title: The three muscle types and how muscles work together
blurb: Tell skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle apart, name agonist, antagonist, origin and insertion, and match major muscles to their actions.
question: During a biceps curl, one arm muscle shortens to bend the elbow while another relaxes. Which is the agonist, which is the antagonist, and which attachment of the biceps stays still?

teach.body: Formally, muscle tissue is tissue specialized to contract, and the body has three types: skeletal, cardiac and smooth. In plain English: every muscle cell pulls by shortening, but each type is built for a different setting. Skeletal muscle moves bones on command, cardiac muscle pumps the heart nonstop, and smooth muscle squeezes hollow organs and vessels slowly and steadily, without you thinking about it.

teach.caption: Smooth muscle is also found in the iris and the arrector pili of the skin.
Cardiac muscle resists fatigue, and its long refractory period prevents sustained (tetanic) contraction.

items: Movement of the body and its parts.
Moving substances through the body: blood, food, urine.

teach.body: The agonist (prime mover) performs an action; the antagonist opposes it and relaxes or stretches; a synergist assists; a fixator stabilizes the origin. The origin is the attachment on the more stationary bone and the insertion is on the bone that moves. Tendons attach muscle to bone (an aponeurosis is a broad, flat tendon); ligaments attach bone to bone.

teach.h: Elbow: roles swap with the action
teach.caption: The same muscle can be agonist in one movement and antagonist in the opposite one.

teach.h: Major muscles: head, trunk and arm

teach.body: Tyler, a pre-nursing student, curls a dumbbell. His biceps brachii is the agonist: it contracts to flex the elbow. His triceps brachii is the antagonist and relaxes. The biceps origin, on the stable shoulder end, stays put while its insertion on the forearm moves. Later, when he straightens his elbow against a cable in a triceps push-down, the triceps is the agonist for extension and the biceps becomes its antagonist.

teach.text: Cardiac muscle IS striated and involuntary; smooth muscle is NOT striated. Intercalated discs are CARDIAC only. Biceps FLEXES the elbow, quadriceps EXTENDS the knee. The INSERTION is the end that moves. Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.

items: Skeletal: striated, voluntary, multinucleated. Cardiac: striated, involuntary, intercalated discs. Smooth: non-striated, involuntary, spindle-shaped.
Functions: movement, posture, joint stability, heat, moving substances, protection.
Agonist acts, antagonist opposes, synergist assists, fixator stabilizes.
Origin on the stationary bone; insertion on the moving bone.
Deltoid abducts arm; biceps flexes and triceps extends elbow; quadriceps extends and hamstrings flex knee.

summary: You can now distinguish skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle by location, striation, control and cell shape, and list what muscles do. You can also assign agonist, antagonist, synergist and fixator roles, locate origin and insertion, and match major muscles to their actions.

A.q: Which muscle type is striated but involuntary?
A.why: Cardiac muscle has striations like skeletal muscle but is involuntary; it is autorhythmic, and the ANS adjusts its rate.

whyNot.0: Skeletal muscle is striated but voluntary.
whyNot.1: Smooth muscle is involuntary but not striated.
whyNot.3: Smooth muscle lacks striations, so only cardiac fits both features.

A.q: Intercalated discs, which link cells electrically and mechanically, are found in which muscle type?
A.why: Intercalated discs, made of gap junctions and desmosomes, join branched cardiac muscle cells.

whyNot.0: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated cells without intercalated discs.
whyNot.2: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped and lack intercalated discs.
whyNot.3: Intercalated discs are found in cardiac muscle and not in skeletal muscle.

A.q: Which structure attaches a skeletal muscle to a bone?
A.why: Tendons attach muscle to bone; a broad, flat tendon is an aponeurosis.

whyNot.1: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers inside the muscle.
whyNot.2: The synovial capsule encloses a freely movable joint; it does not anchor muscle.

B.q: During elbow flexion, which muscle acts as the antagonist?
B.why: The biceps brachii flexes the elbow as agonist; the triceps brachii opposes that movement, so it is the antagonist.

whyNot.0: The biceps brachii is the agonist (prime mover) for elbow flexion.
whyNot.1: The deltoid abducts the arm at the shoulder; it does not oppose elbow flexion.
whyNot.2: Pectoralis major moves the arm at the shoulder, not the elbow.

B.q: Which muscle is correctly paired with its main action?
B.why: The deltoid abducts the arm, lifting it away from the body's midline.

whyNot.1: The biceps brachii flexes the elbow; the triceps extends it.
whyNot.2: The quadriceps femoris extends the knee; the hamstrings flex it.
whyNot.3: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes the foot; gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex it.

B.q: Which phrase best describes the origin of a skeletal muscle?
options: Lies on the bone that moves
Stays on the more stationary bone
Lies at the distal end of the limb
Joins the muscle to its antagonist
B.why: The origin is the attachment to the more stationary bone; the insertion is on the bone that moves.

whyNot.0: The attachment on the bone that moves is the insertion.
whyNot.2: The origin is defined by being on the more stationary bone; distal limb attachments are usually insertions.
whyNot.3: Origins attach muscle to bone, not to another muscle.

C.q: Tyler slowly curls a dumbbell up toward his shoulder. Which statement is correct?
options: Triceps is the agonist; biceps relaxes as the antagonist
Biceps is the agonist; its origin is on the bone that moves
Biceps and triceps both contract together as synergists
Biceps is the agonist; triceps relaxes as the antagonist
C.why: Curling flexes the elbow: the biceps brachii is the prime mover and the triceps brachii, which extends the elbow, is the antagonist.

whyNot.0: The triceps extends the elbow, so it cannot be the prime mover of a curl.
whyNot.1: The origin is on the stationary bone; the biceps insertion is the end that moves the forearm.
whyNot.2: Opposing muscles do not both act as synergists; the triceps opposes flexion.

C.q: Which feature distinguishes smooth muscle from BOTH skeletal and cardiac muscle?
options: Its cells have a single nucleus
It contracts using actin and myosin
C.why: Skeletal and cardiac muscle are both striated; smooth muscle is the only non-striated type.

whyNot.0: Cardiac muscle is also involuntary, so this does not separate smooth from cardiac.
whyNot.2: Cardiac cells usually have one nucleus too, so this does not separate smooth from cardiac.
whyNot.3: All three types contract using actin and myosin.

C.q: A patient in a cold room begins to shiver. Which muscle function is this, and which muscle type performs it?
C.why: Shivering is rapid contraction of skeletal muscle, and its purpose is heat production.

whyNot.1: Smooth muscle in the skin raises hairs (arrector pili), but shivering is skeletal muscle.
whyNot.2: Skeletal muscle does maintain posture, but shivering serves heat production.
whyNot.3: Moving substances (blood, food, urine) is a smooth-muscle role, not the purpose of shivering.

reteach.title: Muscles as ropes on a drawbridge
reteach.question: A drawbridge is raised by one rope and lowered by another on the opposite side. How does that explain why muscles come in opposing pairs?

blocks.body: A muscle does its work by contracting, so it can only pull on its tendon, like a rope. To raise the forearm, the front rope (biceps) pulls while the back rope (triceps) lets out slack. To straighten the arm against resistance, the back rope (triceps) pulls and the front one lets out. The post the rope is tied to on land is the origin; the end tied to the moving bridge is the insertion.

blocks.text: Roles belong to the movement, not the muscle: in extension the triceps is the agonist and the biceps the antagonist.

explain.body: Skeletal: attached to bones, striated, voluntary, long multinucleated fibers. Cardiac: heart wall only, striated, involuntary, branched cells joined by intercalated discs. Smooth: walls of hollow organs, vessels and airways, non-striated, involuntary, spindle-shaped.

test.q: Which muscle type forms the walls of blood vessels and hollow organs?
test.why: Smooth muscle forms the walls of hollow organs, blood vessels and airways, producing slow, sustained contractions such as peristalsis.

whyNot.1: Cardiac muscle is found in the heart wall only.
whyNot.3: Striated muscle means skeletal and cardiac; vessel and organ walls are non-striated.

explain.body: Muscles move the body, maintain posture, stabilize joints, produce heat (shivering), move substances such as blood, food and urine, and protect organs.

test.q: Which is NOT a function of the muscular system?
test.why: Blood cells are produced in red bone marrow, a skeletal-system function.

whyNot.0: Muscle contraction produces heat; shivering is an example.
whyNot.2: Muscles that cross a joint help hold it stable.

explain.body: Agonist (prime mover) does the action. Antagonist opposes it. Synergist assists the agonist. Fixator stabilizes the origin so the agonist pulls efficiently. Origin = stationary attachment; insertion = moving attachment.

test.q: Which muscle role stabilizes the origin so the prime mover can act efficiently?
test.why: A fixator holds the origin steady, giving the prime mover a firm anchor.

whyNot.0: A synergist assists the agonist with the movement itself.
whyNot.3: The agonist is the prime mover that performs the action.

explain.body: Diaphragm: inspiration. Deltoid: abducts arm. Biceps: flexes elbow; triceps: extends it. Gluteus maximus: extends hip. Quadriceps: extends knee; hamstrings: flex it. Gastrocnemius and soleus: plantar flexion; tibialis anterior: dorsiflexion. Masseter: closes jaw.

test.q: Which muscle is the main muscle of inspiration?
test.why: The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration, assisted by the external intercostals.

whyNot.2: The internal intercostals act in forced expiration.
whyNot.3: The sternocleidomastoid flexes and rotates the head.
